Cookie consent for plant operator portals

Operator portals that reach outside the plant network fall under the same consent rules as any public website, and the exemption most integrators assume applies to them does not. This note sets out what a portal must ask for, what it may store without asking, and where the boundary sits for a session that spans a shift change.

What counts as strictly necessary

A cookie is strictly necessary when the service the operator asked for cannot be delivered without it. Authentication, load balancing and the CSRF token all qualify. Anything that measures how a page is used does not, however carefully it is anonymised, and a banner that says we use cookies to improve your experience is describing measurement rather than necessity.

The practical consequence is that a portal can keep an operator signed in across a shift change without asking, but cannot record which screens that operator visited without a positive choice. Our own privacy policy separates the two for exactly this reason, and the manage preferences screen in the portal shows the operator which category each cookie falls into.

Where portals usually get it wrong

  • Loading the analytics tag before the choice is made, so the first page view is recorded whatever the operator then decides.
  • Treating an accept all click on the corporate website as consent for the portal, which is a different controller and a different purpose.
  • Storing the consent record itself for longer than the consent lasts, which turns a compliance artefact into a retention problem.

Further reading

  • Portal consent configuration — how to stage the tag loader behind the consent record, with the two settings that most deployments miss.
  • Retention windows — the default retention for each cookie category the portal sets, and how to shorten them per site.
  • Consent audit export — producing the evidence pack an auditor asks for without exporting operator identities.
